tip: The internet fell: έπεσε το ίντερνετ (épese to ínternet) – Greek services fall when they go down. Power too: έπεσε το ρεύμα (épese to révma).
The battery finished, not you: μου τελείωσε η μπαταρία (mou telíose i bataría) – 'it ran out on me'. μου (mou) marks who it happened to.
Downloads come down: κατέβασε (katévase) is literally 'bring it down'. Same verb for downloading apps, songs and files.
ανέβασα (anévasa) = 'I put up' – the same verb that uploads videos also raises speed: ανέβασα την ταχύτητα (anévasa tin tachítita).
Greek keeps files in an actual cloud: στο σύννεφο (sto sínefo) is the same word as the ones in the sky – no separate tech term.
English verbs join Greek with -άρω (-áro): μπλόκαρα (blókara) = I blocked. Also ποστάρω (postáro = post), σερφάρω (serfáro = surf).
The line got cut: κόπηκε η γραμμή (kópike i grammí) is the set phrase for a dropped call – nobody 'drops' anything in Greek.
Greek closes what English turns off: έκλεισα τις ειδοποιήσεις (éklisa tis idopiísis) – κλείνω (klíno) works for lights, phones and sound too.
Όλα τα βλέπω (óla ta vlépo) names the object twice – όλα, then the little τα (ta). Starting with the object needs that echo; it's required, not sloppy.
No 'of' after boredom: το βαριέμαι (to variéme) takes a plain object – you're bored something in Greek, not bored of it.
You enter your account in Greek: μπήκα στον λογαριασμό (bíka ston logariasmó). μπαίνω (béno) covers logging in and joining wi-fi.
Greek phones strike, they don't ring: χτυπάει (chtipái) is the hit verb – doorbells and alarm clocks χτυπάνε (chtipáne) too.
Loanwords don't change shape: πολλά λάικ (pollá láik) has no plural ending – λάικ (láik) stays the same however many you get.
